q: A buyer agency agreement mainly:
options: Creates an agency relationship and states the broker's duties and pay
Obligates the seller to pay the buyer's broker
Guarantees the buyer will find a home
wrong: The seller isn't a party to the buyer's agreement.
Only a deed transfers title.
No agreement can guarantee an outcome.
why: The buyer agreement sets up the agency and spells out duties, term, and compensation.
hook: Put the buyer's relationship on paper.

q: Under an exclusive buyer agency agreement, the buyer finds and buys a home on their own during the term. The broker is generally:
options: Owed a referral fee by the seller
Owed compensation only if they showed that home
wrong: Exclusive means the broker is paid if the buyer buys during the term.
The seller has no agreement with the buyer's broker.
Showing the specific home isn't required under an exclusive agreement.
why: An exclusive buyer agreement usually pays the broker if the buyer purchases during the term, however the home was found.
hook: Exclusive means one broker, paid either way.

q: Under a nonexclusive buyer agreement, a broker is usually paid only if:
options: The broker is the procuring cause of the purchase
The buyer buys anything during the term
wrong: That describes an exclusive agreement.
The seller's agreement isn't the trigger.
Financing isn't the trigger.
why: Nonexclusive agreements let buyers use other brokers, so payment follows procuring cause.
hook: Nonexclusive: bring the deal, get paid.

q: A buyer agreement promises the broker 2.5%. The seller offers buyer brokers 2%. Under a typical agreement, the remaining 0.5%:
options: May be owed by the buyer, as the agreement states
Must be paid by the listing agent
Is paid by the title company
wrong: Nothing waives it unless the agreement says so.
The listing agent isn't party to the buyer agreement.
Title companies don't owe commissions.
why: The buyer agreement controls the buyer broker's compensation; if the seller pays less, the buyer may owe the difference.
hook: Who pays, how much, and when: write it down.

q: A buyer wants to tour homes today and asks what they're signing in your buyer agreement. What should the agent do?
options: Walk through the term, the duties, and exactly how and how much the broker will be paid, and answer questions before they sign
Say it's a standard form and they don't need to read it
Let them tour first and explain the agreement after they've chosen a home
Tell them the seller always pays so the terms don't matter
wrong: Waving off a contract's terms fails the duty to disclose.
Material terms belong at the start, not after decisions are made.
That's not always true and misstates the agreement.
why: The buyer should understand the agreement, especially compensation, before signing.
hook: Explain it before they sign it.

q: Which term is most important to include so a buyer agreement doesn't run forever?
wrong: Credit details don't set the term.
The buyer agreement isn't tied to one listing.
No specific home is known when it's signed.
why: A clear expiration date defines how long the relationship and obligations last.
hook: Every agreement needs an end date.

q: A business hires a broker to find office space to lease. The agreement is best called a:
wrong: That's for selling property.
An option gives a right to buy on set terms.
Property management is for owners, not tenants.
why: Tenant representation agreements hire a broker to represent someone seeking to lease.
hook: Tenants can hire representation too.

q: A buyer agreement expires March 1. On March 20 the buyer buys a home the broker showed in February, and the agreement has a 60-day protection clause. The broker is most likely:
options: Owed compensation only from the seller
Owed only if the buyer re-signs
wrong: The protection period covers homes shown during the term.
Who pays depends on the agreement; the buyer may owe it.
No new signature is needed for the protection clause to apply.
why: Like listings, buyer agreements often include a protection period for properties shown during the term.
hook: Introduced it? You're protected.

q: A buyer's broker can be paid by the seller and still represent the buyer.
wrong: Who pays does not determine whom the broker represents.
why: True. Agency depends on the relationship, not the source of payment.
hook: Payment doesn't decide loyalty.

q: Relying on an oral buyer agreement makes it easier for a broker to collect compensation in a dispute.
wrong: Oral agreements are hard to prove and may be unenforceable for commissions. Written agreements protect everyone.
why: False. Written agreements make terms provable and enforceable.
hook: If it isn't written, it's hard to collect.

q: Once a buyer agency agreement is signed, the broker owes the buyer:
options: Only honesty, the same as any customer
Duties only if the seller agrees
wrong: A client is owed more than a customer: full fiduciary duties.
Duties begin when the agency begins.
The seller's consent isn't needed.
why: The buyer becomes the broker's client, owed fiduciary duties.
hook: Sign the agreement, gain a client.

q: A buyer agreement promises the broker 2.5% of the price. The home sells for $460,000 and the seller pays the buyer's broker 2%. How much does the buyer owe the broker to make up the difference?
formula: Shortfall = price × (agreed rate − rate paid by seller)
why: The gap is 0.5% of $460,000, which is $2,300.
hook: Who pays, how much, and when: write it down.

q: A represented buyer loves a for-sale-by-owner home. The buyer's broker should:
options: Help the buyer pursue it and resolve compensation as the buyer agreement provides
Refuse to show it because no commission is offered
Tell the buyer it's illegal to buy without a listing
Ask the seller to sign an exclusive right to sell listing first
wrong: Steering a client away from a home over commission puts the broker's interests first.
Buying from an owner directly is legal.
The buyer's broker doesn't need a listing to help the buyer.
why: A buyer's broker serves the buyer. The buyer agreement covers compensation when the seller pays nothing.
hook: The client's interest comes before the commission.

q: Like a listing, a buyer agency agreement ends:
options: On performance, expiration, mutual agreement, or by operation of law
wrong: There are several ways it can end besides closing.
Death of either party is just one way.
Agreements always have ways to end.
why: Agency agreements end the same ways: performance, expiration, agreement, or operation of law.
hook: Every agreement has an exit.

q: Compensation in a buyer agreement is negotiable between the buyer and the broker.
wrong: Commissions are always negotiable; no law sets them.
why: True. Commissions are set by negotiation, not by law or by groups of brokers.
hook: Every commission is negotiable.

q: A buyer under an exclusive agreement wants to see a home listed by the same brokerage. Before going further, the brokerage must:
options: Disclose the relationship and get the required informed consent from both parties
Ask the seller to cancel the listing
wrong: Refusing isn't required; consent and disclosure are.
There's no need to cancel; disclosure and consent are the path forward.
The listing doesn't need to be canceled.
why: Representing both sides requires disclosure and informed consent, as state law sets out.
hook: Two clients, one firm: disclose and get consent.

q: A seller responds to an offer by changing only the closing date. Legally, the seller has:
options: Rejected the offer and made a counteroffer
Made a binding contract with a new date
wrong: Acceptance must match the offer exactly.
No contract exists until the buyer accepts the new terms.
An option is a separate contract.
why: Any change is a counteroffer, which rejects the original offer.
hook: Change anything, and you've rejected everything.

q: A buyer can withdraw an offer:
options: Any time before acceptance is communicated
wrong: The offeror controls the offer until acceptance.
A written offer can still be revoked before acceptance.
Inspection timing has nothing to do with revocation.
why: An offer can be revoked before the offeror learns it has been accepted.
hook: No acceptance yet? Still yours to take back.

q: After signing a purchase agreement but before closing, the buyer holds:
wrong: Legal title passes at closing by deed.
A life estate is a freehold measured by a life.
The buyer has an enforceable interest.
why: A buyer under contract holds equitable title until legal title passes at closing.
hook: Signed contract: equitable now, legal later.

q: Earnest money is best described as:
options: A good-faith deposit held in trust and usually credited to the buyer at closing
A required down payment set by law
A fee paid to the seller that's never refunded
wrong: It belongs to the transaction, not the broker.
No law sets a required amount.
It's often refundable if a contingency isn't met.
why: Earnest money shows good faith, is held in trust, and is usually applied to the buyer's costs at closing.
hook: Earnest money: proof you're serious.

q: A buyer with a financing contingency is denied a loan despite applying in good faith. Usually the buyer can:
options: Cancel and get the earnest money back
wrong: The contingency excuses performance.
That's the risk the contingency protects against.
Nothing requires paying cash.
why: A financing contingency lets the buyer exit if the loan isn't approved, as the contract describes.
hook: Contingency: if this, then that.

q: A buyer makes an offer and dies before the seller accepts. The offer:
options: Passes to the buyer's estate to accept
Becomes binding when the seller signs
wrong: Offers don't pass to estates.
There's no offer left to accept.
Nothing converts it.
why: An offer ends on the death or incapacity of either party before acceptance.
hook: An offer dies with its maker.

q: You receive a lowball offer an hour after presenting a strong one, and the seller hasn't responded yet. What should the agent do?
options: Present the new offer to the seller promptly
Hold it until the strong offer is resolved
Reject it because it's too low
Tell the buyer's agent it's pointless
wrong: Withholding offers takes the decision away from the seller.
Only the seller can reject an offer.
Dismissing it on the seller's behalf oversteps the agent's role.
why: Agents present all offers to the seller promptly. The seller decides.
hook: Present every offer. The seller picks.

q: A seller signs the buyer's offer but, before telling anyone, the buyer calls to withdraw. Most likely:
options: The offer was withdrawn before acceptance was communicated, so there's no contract
A contract exists because the seller signed
The buyer forfeits the earnest money
The seller can sue for specific performance
wrong: Signing alone isn't enough; acceptance must be communicated.
Without a contract, there's nothing to forfeit.
No contract exists to enforce.
why: Acceptance must be communicated to the offeror. The buyer revoked first.
hook: Accepted but unsaid isn't accepted.

q: A counteroffer is a new offer that the original offeror may accept or reject.
wrong: That's right: the roles flip with each counter.
why: True.
hook: Each counter flips the roles.

q: After a seller counteroffers, the buyer can still accept the original offer the seller rejected.
wrong: The counteroffer rejected the original offer. It's gone unless someone makes it again.
why: False. A counteroffer kills the original offer.
hook: Change anything, and you've rejected everything.

q: A buyer is purchasing a $350,000 home with a 10% down payment and has already deposited $5,000 earnest money that will be credited. How much more cash does the buyer need for the down payment at closing, ignoring closing costs?
formula: Additional cash = (price × down payment %) − earnest money
why: The $5,000 deposit is credited toward the $35,000 down payment, leaving $30,000.
hook: Earnest money is credited back to the buyer.

q: Which contingency lets a buyer exit or renegotiate after reviewing the home's condition?
wrong: That's about loan approval.
That depends on selling the buyer's current home.
That's about the condition of title, not the house.
why: An inspection (due diligence) contingency covers the property's physical condition.
hook: Inspection: look before you're locked in.

q: A seller sends identical counteroffers to two buyers at the same time. The biggest risk is:
options: Both buyers accept, creating two binding contracts
wrong: Both can respond; that's the problem.
The listing continues.
Earnest money isn't affected.
why: Multiple simultaneous counteroffers can each be accepted, leaving the seller bound twice. They should be worded to prevent that.
hook: Counter two at once, risk selling twice.

q: Put these steps in the order they happen when a counteroffer is accepted.
options: Buyer signs and delivers an offer
Seller changes the price and signs a counteroffer
Seller learns the counteroffer was accepted, and a contract exists
why: An offer, a counter that rejects it, acceptance of the counter, and communication of that acceptance form the contract.
hook: Offer, counter, accept, tell.

q: Earnest money a broker receives must be handled as trust funds, not mixed with the broker's own money.
wrong: Mixing client money with the broker's own is commingling, which is prohibited.
why: True. Earnest money belongs to the transaction, not the broker.
hook: Their money, separate account.

q: To create a contract, an acceptance must be:
options: Unconditional and match the offer's terms
wrong: Notarization isn't required for acceptance.
Title insurance isn't part of acceptance.
Recording isn't required for a contract to form.
why: Acceptance must agree to every term without conditions; otherwise it's a counteroffer.
hook: Mirror the offer exactly.

q: In an option to purchase, which party is obligated to complete the sale if the option is exercised?
options: Both, from the day it's signed
wrong: The optionee may choose not to buy.
Only the owner is bound before exercise.
The owner is bound.
why: The optionor must sell on the agreed terms if the optionee exercises; the optionee is free to walk away.
hook: The optionee has the option. The optionor is bound.

q: For an option to be enforceable, the optionee must generally:
wrong: Option periods vary by agreement.
Recording gives notice but isn't required between the parties.
Financing isn't required to hold an option.
why: An option is a contract, so the optionee must give consideration, such as an option fee.
hook: Pay for the right to decide.

q: An option is what kind of contract until it's exercised?
wrong: Only the owner promises; the optionee doesn't promise to buy.
A properly made option is valid.
Nothing has been performed yet.
why: Only the optionor makes a promise, so an option is unilateral until exercised.
hook: Uni means one promises.

q: A right of first refusal gives the holder the right to:
options: Match a third party's offer before the owner accepts it
Buy at a fixed price whenever they want
wrong: That describes an option.
The owner can choose not to sell at all.
It's a purchase right, not a commission.
why: The holder gets the first chance to match a real offer.
hook: First refusal: match it or lose it.

q: Under a land contract, who holds legal title until the price is paid in full?
wrong: The buyer holds equitable title and possession.
That describes a deed of trust, not a land contract.
The county doesn't hold title.
why: The vendor keeps legal title until the last installment is paid.
hook: Pay it all, then the deed falls.

q: A developer holds an option on a lot and wants to sell the option to another builder. Generally the option:
options: Can be assigned unless the option agreement prohibits it
Can be assigned only after it's exercised
wrong: Options are generally assignable.
Assignment can happen before exercise.
Assignment doesn't end it.
why: Options are generally assignable unless the agreement says otherwise.
hook: Assignable unless it says no.

q: A tenant signs a lease that also gives them the right to buy the home at a set price within two years. This is a:
options: Lease with an option to purchase
wrong: A land contract is a sale with installment payments.
A right of first refusal has no set price.
Novation replaces a contract.
why: A lease combined with an option gives the tenant the right, not the duty, to buy.
hook: Lease now, option to own.

q: You list a home whose tenant has a right of first refusal in the lease. You receive an acceptable offer. What should the agent do?
options: Make sure the seller notifies the tenant of the offer terms as the lease requires before accepting it
Accept the offer and tell the tenant later
Ignore the lease because the listing came later
Tell the buyer the tenant's right is void
wrong: Accepting first could breach the tenant's right.
A recorded or known right of first refusal binds the owner.
The agent can't declare a contract right void.
why: The tenant must get the chance to match before the seller accepts.
hook: First refusal: match it or lose it.

q: An optionee who decides not to buy loses the option fee but owes nothing more.
wrong: Letting an option expire is the optionee's right. They lose only what they paid for it.
why: True. The fee paid for the right, not for the property.
hook: Pay for the right to decide.

q: A right of first refusal usually sets the price the holder will pay.
wrong: A right of first refusal follows the price in a third party's offer. A fixed price is a feature of an option.
why: False. The holder matches whatever offer comes in.
hook: First refusal: match it or lose it.

q: In a land contract, the buyer usually takes possession before receiving the deed.
wrong: The buyer moves in and pays installments; the deed comes later.
why: True.
hook: Live there now, deed later.

q: A buyer pays a $6,000 option fee, which the contract credits toward the $240,000 purchase price. The buyer exercises the option. How much of the price remains to be paid?
why: The credited option fee reduces the remaining price to $234,000.
hook: Credited fees come off the top.

q: A buyer purchases land for $90,000 on a land contract with $10,000 down. Ignoring interest, after 48 monthly principal payments of $500, what principal balance remains?
formula: Balance = price − down payment − (payments × principal per payment)
why: $80,000 financed minus $24,000 paid leaves $56,000.
hook: Pay it all, then the deed falls.

q: If the optionee doesn't exercise an option before the deadline, the option:
options: Expires, and the optionor keeps the option fee
Becomes a right of first refusal
wrong: It doesn't convert into another right.
Nobody is obligated to buy.
Extensions must be agreed.
why: An unexercised option simply ends; the fee usually stays with the owner.
hook: Miss the window, lose the option.

q: Which is a significant risk for a buyer under a land contract?
options: The seller still holds legal title and could encumber it or fail to deliver a clear deed
The buyer can never get title
The buyer can't live in the home
The buyer must pay a broker twice
wrong: The buyer gets title after paying in full.
Buyers usually take possession.
There's no double commission.
why: Because the vendor keeps legal title, liens or the vendor's problems can cloud title. Buyers often record the contract and get title review.
hook: Seller keeps the deed, buyer keeps the risk.

q: A land contract is also called a:
options: Contract for deed or installment sales contract
wrong: A deed of trust secures a loan with a trustee holding title.
A lease option is a lease with a right to buy.
A quitclaim is a deed.
why: Land contract, contract for deed, and installment sales contract describe the same arrangement.
hook: Contract for deed: the deed comes at the end.
